did_you_know.text: Did you know? Naboth’s vineyard was near Ahab’s palace in Jezreel, although Ahab is described here as the king of Samaria.
Did you know? Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard because he regards it as his ancestral inheritance, and therefore he is unwilling to give it to Ahab.
Did you know? After Naboth refuses, Ahab will not eat, lies on his bed, and turns his face away—a reaction that shows how intensely he desired the vineyard.
Did you know? Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal, using the king’s authority to carry out her plot.

Did you know? The plot against Naboth was made to look like a public religious proceeding: a fast was proclaimed, Naboth was seated at the head of the people, and two men were required to testify against him.
Did you know? After Naboth was stoned, the men of the city sent Jezebel a brief message: “Naboth has been stoned and is dead.” Only afterward did she tell Ahab that the vineyard was available.

Did you know? Ahab went down to Naboth’s vineyard to take possession of it as soon as he heard that Naboth was dead; thus, the connection between Naboth’s death and the acquisition of the vineyard becomes clear.
Did you know? Elijah’s rebuke of Ahab sums up the essence of his sin in the words: “Have you murdered and also taken possession?”—murder followed by taking the victim’s property.
Did you know? When Ahab heard Elijah’s words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and walked about subdued—signs of mourning and submission.
Did you know? Because Ahab humbled himself, the LORD postpones bringing disaster on his household: the punishment will not come in his lifetime, but in the days of his son.
